```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Exercise 1.1: Random sample from the t(4) distribution

A random sample of 100 values is generated from the t distribution with 4 degrees of freedom using `rt`, and displayed as a probability histogram with `MASS::truehist`.

```{r ex-1-1}
set.seed(123)
x <- rt(100, df = 4)
MASS::truehist(x, main = "Sample from t(4)")
```

## Exercise 1.2: Add the t(4) density curve

The true t(4) density (`dt`) is added to the histogram using `curve` with `add = TRUE`.

```{r ex-1-2}
MASS::truehist(x, main = "Sample from t(4) with true density")
curve(dt(x, df = 4), add = TRUE)
```

## Exercise 1.3: Add the estimated density curve

The kernel density estimate from `density` is added in red. It approximates the true t(4) density.

```{r ex-1-3}
MASS::truehist(x, main = "Histogram, true density and estimated density")
curve(dt(x, df = 4), add = TRUE)
lines(density(x), col = 2)
```

The red estimated curve roughly follows the black true density curve.

## Exercise 1.4: Transformation function

**(a)** The function `f` transforms a vector `x` by subtracting `a` and dividing by `b`.

```{r ex-1-4a}
f <- function(x, a, b) {
  (x - a) / b
}
```

**(b)** A Normal(2, 2) sample is transformed to the interval [0, 1].

```{r ex-1-4b}
set.seed(123)
x <- rnorm(100, mean = 2, sd = 2)
y <- f(x, a = min(x), b = max(x) - min(x))
summary(x)
summary(y)
```

The transformed sample `y` has a minimum of 0 and a maximum of 1.

## Exercise 1.5: Studentize the sample

The sample is centered by its mean and scaled by its standard deviation.

```{r ex-1-5}
z <- f(x, a = mean(x), b = sd(x))
summary(z)
hist(z, main = "Studentized sample z")
sd(z)
```

The mean of `z` is 0 (up to rounding error) and the standard deviation is exactly 1.

## Exercise 1.6: Center by median, scale by IQR

```{r ex-1-6}
w <- f(x, a = median(x), b = IQR(x))
summary(w)
hist(w, main = "Median/IQR scaled sample w")
sd(w)
```

Compared with Exercise 1.5, the median of `w` is exactly 0 and its IQR is 1, but its mean is not exactly 0 and its standard deviation is not 1. The median and IQR are less affected by outliers than the mean and standard deviation.

## Exercise 1.7: ggplot with color = drv

Adding `color = drv` inside `aes()` colors the points by drive type (front-wheel, rear-wheel, four-wheel) and automatically creates a legend.

```{r ex-1-7}
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ class)
```

## Exercise 1.8: Examples 1.12 and 1.14

### Example 1.12: A minimal ggplot scatterplot

This example introduces `ggplot`. The first version specifies the data (`iris`), maps `Sepal.Length` to the x axis and `Sepal.Width` to the y axis, and draws the points with `geom_point()`. In this version all three species have the same color, so the effect of species cannot be seen.

```{r example-1-12a}
ggplot(data = iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point()
```

The second version adds aesthetics that map `Species` to both color and plotting symbol, and sets the symbol size to 2. A legend is added to the graph automatically, so the three species can be distinguished.

```{r example-1-12b}
ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width,
                 color = Species, shape = Species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2)
```

### Example 1.14: MPG by engine displacement

This example uses the `mpg` data from the `ggplot2` package. It plots highway mileage (`hwy`) against engine displacement (`displ`) for each class of vehicle. `facet_wrap(~ class)` splits the plot into an array of panels, one per class, with identical x and y axes so they are easy to compare.

```{r example-1-14}
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ class)
```
